title: Effects of multisystemic therapy through midlife: a 21.9-year follow-up to a randomized clinical trial with serious and violent juvenile offenders
authors: Aaron M. Sawyer; Charles M. Borduin
publication: Journal of Consulting and Clinical Psychology 79(5):643-652
access_status: publisher and PubMed primary records, author-supplied article preview, DOI, and underlying thesis record inspected
evidence_scope: Intent-to-treat follow-up of 176 people originally randomized as adolescents to multisystemic therapy or individual therapy; official criminal and civil records obtained a mean 21.9 years after treatment
sequence_allegation: serious and violent juvenile offending; mean 3.9 prior felony arrests
sequence_assessment: juvenile-court referral and the original randomized clinical-trial assessment
sequence_intervention: family- and community-based multisystemic therapy versus individual therapy
sequence_review: official-record follow-ups from the original trial through middle adulthood
sequence_later_outcome: felony recidivism 34.8% versus 54.8%; misdemeanor frequency 5.0 times lower in MST; family-related civil-suit odds twice as high after individual therapy
notes: Exceptionally long outcome window, but one developer-led trial; Charles Borduin disclosed membership on the board of MST Associates LLC. Records do not measure victim safety, wellbeing, family burden, or which treatment or transition component caused the difference

lane: adjacent family and home-based child-welfare effectiveness
title: Effects of functional family therapy for adolescents in child welfare services on subsequent criminal charges and out-of-home placements: a randomized effectiveness trial
authors: Asgeir Røyrhus Olseth; Andreas Høstmælingen; Gunnar Bjørnebekk
access_status: complete open primary article, tables, protocol deviations, limitations, funding, conflict disclosure, DOI, and trial-registration link inspected
evidence_scope: Randomized effectiveness trial in regular Norwegian child-welfare services; national-registry outcomes for 129 youths at 18 and 36 months after intake
sequence_allegation: disruptive, aggressive, violent, school, or placement-risk referrals; few participants had prior charges
sequence_assessment: child-welfare eligibility, baseline measures, random assignment, and national-identifier linkage
sequence_intervention: three-to-six-month functional family therapy versus active treatment as usual, including MST, parent training, and family counselling
sequence_review: implementation fidelity monitoring plus national-registry follow-up; protocol and control services changed during recruitment
sequence_later_outcome: no statistically significant difference in criminal charges at 18 or 36 months or out-of-home placement at 18 months
notes: Underpowered registry subset and active heterogeneous comparator; 40.7% of TAU received MST and TAU averaged more treatment hours. Two authors worked for the government-funded organization that implemented FFT in Norway from 2007 to 2024

lane: adjacent treatment foster care versus group care durability
title: Multidimensional Treatment Foster Care for Girls in the Juvenile Justice System: 2-Year Follow-up of a Randomized Clinical Trial
authors: Patricia Chamberlain; Leslie D. Leve; David S. DeGarmo
publication: Journal of Consulting and Clinical Psychology 75(1):187-193
access_status: complete open primary author manuscript, PubMed and PMC records, methods, results, limitations, DOI, and CONSORT flow inspected
evidence_scope: Intent-to-treat randomized comparison of treatment foster care and 19 community group-care programs for 81 girls with chronic delinquency; 12- and 24-month follow-up
sequence_allegation: juvenile-court mandate to out-of-home care; mean more than 11 criminal referrals at baseline
sequence_assessment: baseline court, youth, caregiver, and demographic assessment
sequence_intervention: trained and supervised foster homes with daily monitoring, caregiver support, youth and family therapy, school coordination, and on-call consultation versus usual group care
sequence_review: daily and weekly fidelity and case review during placement; blinded 12- and 24-month assessments and court records
sequence_later_outcome: greater reduction in the 24-month delinquency construct for MTFC; standardized beta -0.36 and Cohen's d 0.65; more than 100 fewer locked-setting days in raw means
notes: Mean randomized-placement stay was 174 days, so much of the 24-month window was beyond placement. Small, mostly White regional sample; developer-affiliated team; no component isolation, victim outcome, family-burden outcome, or independent replication in this source

lane: adjacent residential forensic treatment and post-release transition
title: Effectiveness of an Individual Cognitive-Behavioral Intervention for Serious, Young Male Violent Offenders: Randomized Controlled Study With Twenty-Four-Month Follow-Up
authors: Martin Lardén; Jens Högström; Niklas Långström
access_status: complete open primary article, tables, supplement link, limitations, conflict disclosure, DOI, and PMC record inspected
evidence_scope: Five-site randomized effectiveness trial in Swedish residential treatment homes; 81 males aged 16-21 assessed at 12 and 24 months after release
sequence_allegation: conviction for serious violent crime and medium-to-high assessed violent-recidivism risk
sequence_assessment: baseline self-report, trained independent assessment, randomization across five sites, and nationwide conviction records
sequence_intervention: 15-to-20-session individual CBT add-on begun four-to-six months before release, including relapse planning and identification of prosocial supports, versus group-based treatment as usual alone
sequence_review: therapist supervision, masked 12-month interviews, and nationwide conviction data for all participants at 12 and 24 months
sequence_later_outcome: no significant added effect on aggression or reconviction; violent reconviction was 34% versus 23% at 12 months and 50% versus 40% at 24 months for iCBT plus TAU versus TAU
notes: Only 15 of 38 assigned to iCBT completed at least 15 sessions and the trial was underpowered. Some participants were legal adults. The first author designed the intervention but reported no royalties, training, consulting, commercial, or financial gain
